If you need semantic matching later—finding "waterproof jacket" when users search "rain gear"—you'd move to vector embeddings (store product embeddings on index, run similarity search at query time). That adds latency and storage but catches intent-based matches full-text alone misses.

The main trade-off: start simple with database FTS, switch to vectors only if the search quality becomes a problem. Premature optimization here burns implementation time for a feature you don't know users will love yet.

What does the current product data structure look like? That shapes whether FTS is even available to you.

At 38k rows on Postgres, I'd skip a dedicated search engine (Elasticsearch/Algolia) — that's infra you don't need yet. Add a generated `tsvector` column over `name`/`description` with a GIN index, then query it with `websearch_to_tsquery` ranked by `ts_rank`, exposed as a new `GET /products/search?q=` route alongside the existing listing endpoint in `routes/products.js`.

Main tradeoff: full-text search handles multi-word relevance and stemming well but won't catch typos or partial-word matches ("wdget" for "widget") — if that matters, pair it with a `pg_trgm` trigram index for fuzzy fallback, at the cost of a second index and a slightly messier query. Given the current size and growth rate, I'd start with plain full-text search and add trigram only if users actually complain about typos.

For seller photo uploads, the typical approach is:

**Client-side:** Phone camera upload → compress/resize in browser (reduce large camera files to ~2MB max) → send to server via multipart form or chunked upload for resilience.

**Server-side:** Receive file → validate (type, size, dimensions) → store in cloud (S3, GCS, Cloudinary) → return URL → save metadata in database (which listing, upload order, maybe metadata like dimensions).

**Key tradeoffs:**

- **Direct-to-cloud upload** (client signs request, uploads directly to S3) is faster and scales better, but requires more client complexity and CORS setup.
- **Server relay** is simpler to implement but uses your server bandwidth; fine for moderate volume.
- **Compression strategy**: Do it on client (save bandwidth, faster perceived upload) vs. server (simpler logic, server stores optimized versions). Client compression is standard now—modern browsers handle it well.
- **Progressive enhancement**: Multiple photos, drag-and-drop, preview before upload, or start simple with one at a time.

The easiest starting point: multipart form POST to your server, store in cloud storage, save the URL in your database. Add client-side compression if uploads feel slow. Scale up to direct-to-cloud or chunked uploads only if you hit bandwidth/reliability issues.

What's the backend stack? That shapes the specific implementation details.

Here's how I'd architect it:

**Capture/selection (client)**
`<input type="file" accept="image/*" capture="environment" multiple>` gets you the native camera or gallery picker on mobile without a custom app. If sellers use a dedicated app, use the native camera API instead for more control (multi-shot, cropping guide).

**Client-side pre-processing — do this before upload, not after**
Phone photos are 3–12MB (or HEIC on iOS, which many backends/browsers don't render). On upload, in-browser:
- Decode and downscale (canvas or a lib like `browser-image-compression`) to something like max 2000–2500px on the long edge — plenty for listing photos, cuts upload size 80%+.
- Convert HEIC → JPEG/WebP if needed.
- Read EXIF orientation, rotate pixels to match, then strip EXIF (GPS/device metadata) before it ever leaves the device — privacy and storage hygiene.

This matters most because sellers are often on cellular with weak upload bandwidth; shrinking client-side is the single biggest win for reliability and speed.

**Transport**
Don't proxy raw image bytes through your app server. Have the backend issue a short-lived presigned URL (S3/GCS/Azure Blob), and upload directly from the client to storage. Backend only handles: auth check, generate presigned URL, then receive a "upload complete" callback (or storage event) to create the DB record. For flaky mobile connections, use resumable/chunked upload (tus protocol, or S3 multipart) so a dropped connection doesn't force a full re-upload.

**Server-side processing (async, triggered by storage event)**
- Generate size variants (thumbnail, card, full) via a worker (sharp/imagemagick) — never resize on the request path.
- Re-validate content-type/magic bytes server-side (never trust client mime type).
- Run moderation/abuse scanning if listings are public-facing.
- Write photo record: `listing_id`, `seller_id`, storage keys per variant, `position` (for ordering), `status` (pending/processed/failed).

**Serving**
CDN in front of the bucket, `srcset` with the generated variants so listing pages don't ship full-res images.

**UX details worth planning for up front**
- Per-photo upload progress + retry-on-failure (uploads will fail on mobile networks).
- Drag-to-reorder and a "set as primary photo" flag.
- Max photo count and per-file size cap enforced both client- and server-side.

Main tradeoff: presigned direct-to-storage upload is more moving parts (client needs upload-then-confirm logic) than just POSTing the file to your API, but it avoids tying up app server workers/bandwidth on large file transfers and scales far better — worth it unless upload volume is tiny.

**The invoices table will block the drop.** It has a foreign key on `user_id` that references `users(id)` with no `ON DELETE CASCADE`, so dropping `users` will fail if any invoices exist.

You'll need to either:

Found the issue. When Redis fails or times out, the `redis.incr()` call in `redis-client.js` (lines 18-23) catches the error and returns `null` instead of throwing.

Back in `limiter.js`, when `count` is `null`:
- Line 13: `if (count === 1)` fails, so the key expiry never gets set
- Line 17: `if (count > MAX_REQUESTS)` fails because `null > 100` is `false`, so the request passes through unchecked

**The culprit:** Redis was likely hitting the 200ms `connectTimeout` (redis-client.js line 5), causing `incr()` to fail and return `null`. This made the rate limiter silently fail-open — every request passed through because `null > 100` is falsy. With a broken Redis connection, all 12,000 requests got through with no rate limiting at all.

The fix would be to make the limiter fail-secure: if `count` is `null`, block the request (or at minimum, know the limiter isn't working). But as requested, I haven't edited anything.

`redis.incr()` swallows every error and returns `null` instead of throwing or rejecting (redis-client.js:18-23). In limiter.js:12-17, `count` becomes `null` whenever that happens, and `null > MAX_REQUESTS` is always `false` — so on any Redis failure (timeout, connection drop, etc.) the request is let through instead of blocked. The `count === 1` check also never matches, so the key's TTL never gets set on that path either.

With `connectTimeout: 200` and `maxRetriesPerRequest: 1` (redis-client.js:5-7), it doesn't take much — one slow/unreachable Redis node for that client's shard — to make every `incr` call fail for a sustained stretch. During that stretch every request for that client bypasses the counter entirely, which is consistent with 12,000 requests in a minute and zero 429s: the limiter was fail-open the whole time, not just occasionally leaking a few over the cap.

`git restore --staged` unstages changes from the staging area while keeping them in your working directory.

For example:
- `git restore --staged file.txt` removes `file.txt` from the staging area but leaves your edits intact in the file
- `git restore --staged .` unstages all staged changes

It's the opposite of `git add` — useful when you've staged something by mistake and want to remove it from the next commit without losing your work.

`git restore --staged <file>` unstages a file — it moves it from the index back to matching your working tree state, without touching the working tree contents. It's the modern equivalent of `git reset HEAD <file>`. Changes in the file itself are kept; only the staging area is affected.

Support multiple keys during a transition window. Here's the pattern:

**During rotation:**
1. Generate a new signing key
2. Add both keys to your signing key store (marked with their activation time and key ID)
3. Start signing new tokens with the new key
4. Include the key ID (`kid`) in JWT headers so your service knows which key validated each token

**Validation:**
- Try to verify incoming tokens against *all* active keys (old and new) until the old key's TTL passes
- Tokens signed with the old key remain valid for their lifetime (usually 24h or less)
- Tokens signed with the new key are immediately valid

**Cleanup:**
- After `max_token_lifetime + grace_period`, remove the old key from validation
- The grace period accounts for clock skew and gives stragglers time to refresh

**Implementation checklist:**
- Store keys with expiry metadata, not just the key material
- Include `kid` in JWT headers (standard practice)
- Query *all* non-expired keys during validation
- Rotate at low-traffic times if possible
- Test with a staging key first

**Common gotchas:**
- Forgetting to include `kid` means you can't tell which key signed a token
- Removing the old key too soon breaks tokens that haven't hit TTL yet
- Clients caching the public key won't see the new one (use JWKS endpoints instead)

Most frameworks (Node.js `jsonwebtoken`, Spring Security, Django) support multiple keys natively—check your stack's docs for the integration pattern.

The standard approach is to support multiple valid signing keys simultaneously during a transition window, rather than a hard cutover.

**1. Key ID (`kid`) in the JWT header**
Every token you issue includes a `kid` claim identifying which key signed it. Your verifier looks up the right public/verification key by `kid` instead of assuming a single global key.

**2. Maintain a key set, not a single key**
Keep a small set of active keys (e.g. `current` for signing new tokens, plus one or more `previous` keys still valid for verification only). If you use asymmetric signing (RS256/ES256), publish this as a JWKS endpoint (`/.well-known/jwks.json`) with each key tagged by `kid`; verifiers fetch and cache it. If you use HMAC (HS256), you'll need to distribute the key set to verifiers directly since there's no public/private split — asymmetric is strongly preferred for rotation because you never have to hand out the signing secret itself.

**3. Rotation sequence**
- Generate a new key, add it to the key set as a *verification-only* key alongside the current one.
- Start signing new tokens with the new key (flip `current`), while still accepting tokens signed by the old key.
- Keep the old key valid for verification until the longest-lived outstanding token issued under it expires (your access token TTL, or refresh token TTL if you sign those too).
- After that window, remove the old key from the set entirely.

This means: don't delete/replace a key outright — retire it only after every token it could have signed has naturally expired. That's what avoids force-logging-out users.

**4. Practical tips**
- Short access-token TTLs (minutes) make rotation windows short and low-risk; long-lived tokens make rotation slower and riskier — if you're on long-lived JWTs, this is a good reason to shorten them and rely on refresh tokens instead.
- Cache JWKS on verifiers but respect cache-control/max-age so new keys propagate promptly; on a `kid` cache-miss, force a refetch before rejecting (handles the case where you rotated and a verifier has a stale cache).
- Automate this (many teams rotate every 30–90 days) with a scheduled job that adds the new key, flips signing, and prunes expired-old keys — I can help build that if you tell me your stack (e.g. what issues the tokens and what library verifies them).

Found it. Line 10 of backup.sh runs the S3 upload in the background with `&`:

```bash
aws s3 cp "$DUMP" "s3://$BACKUP_BUCKET/$STAMP.sql.gz" &
```

Then line 12 immediately deletes the file:

```bash
rm -f "$DUMP"
```

The script exits with the upload still running, so the file gets deleted before S3 finishes reading it. The S3 command fails silently in the background, but the script already logged "backup complete" and exited 0.

You need to either remove the `&` to make the upload synchronous, or add `wait` after the S3 command to wait for the background job before cleaning up.

`aws s3 cp` on line 10 is backgrounded with `&`, so the script doesn't wait for it. It immediately hits `rm -f "$DUMP"` and deletes the dump file, then echoes "backup complete" and exits 0 — likely before the upload finishes, and quite possibly the upload then fails trying to read a file that's already been deleted out from under it (or gets killed when the script/cron job's process group exits). Either way, the exit code and log message only reflect the script's own commands, not the backgrounded `aws s3 cp`, so a failed or truncated upload is silently swallowed.

Fix would be to drop the `&` (or `wait` for the background job before the `rm`).

The 1-hour delay comes from a caching layer between the client and the flag service, not from `flags.js` itself.

**What's happening:**

1. **Client sends a bad directive**: `flags.js` sends `Cache-Control: max-age=3600` in the request header (line 16). This doesn't control how the response gets cached, but it may be misleading Varnish downstream.

2. **Varnish is caching the entire response for 3600 seconds**: Look at the response headers—there's a `via: 1.1 varnish` and `age: 2841` (that's 47 minutes). The `age` header indicates this response has been sitting in the Varnish cache for nearly 47 minutes. The response shows `cache-control: public, max-age=30`, but that only applies *if* the response is served fresh. Once Varnish caches it, Varnish decides when to expire it.

3. **The real TTL is 3600 seconds**: Either Varnish is configured with a 3600-second override for this endpoint, or it's respecting the `max-age=3600` from the client's *request* header (which is not standard but some proxies honor it). Either way, the response sits in Varnish for up to an hour before it asks the flag service for a fresh copy.

The client's 60-second in-process cache is being undercut by Varnish caching upstream. Even if flags.js refetches after 60 seconds, it gets the stale cached version from Varnish instead of hitting the flag service.

Found it — the bug isn't in the in-process cache, it's in the outbound request headers.

- `flags.js:9` correctly re-fetches every 60s once `CACHE_TTL_MS` expires — that part works as intended.
- But every one of those re-fetches sends `Cache-Control: max-age=3600` (`flags.js:16`). That's a *request* directive telling any shared cache in front of the flag service "I'll accept a cached response up to an hour old."
- `response-headers.txt` shows there is such a cache: `via: 1.1 varnish`. The origin itself replies with `cache-control: public, max-age=30` (its own intended freshness), but the observed response has `age: 2841` (~47 min) and `x-cache: HIT` — Varnish is serving a stale hit far past the origin's 30s freshness window, honoring the client's own `max-age=3600` request header instead.

So the 60-second client-side TTL just controls how *often* each service asks — it doesn't control what it gets back. Every ask can still return a Varnish-cached copy up to an hour stale, because `flags.js` itself is the one asking for that staleness. That's why changes still take up to an hour to reach some users: it's bounded by the `max-age=3600` request header in `flags.js`, not by `CACHE_TTL_MS`.

The methodology has merit but has a **critical flaw in the stopping rule** that substantially inflates the false-positive rate.

**The core issue: multiple comparisons and peeking**

The plan says "Each morning we pull the dashboard" and "the first morning any metric shows p < 0.05... we stop." This violates the assumptions of hypothesis testing in two ways:

1. **Multiple metrics**: Checking 8 metrics daily means at each peek, you have ~8 independent tests. With a 5% significance threshold on each, the probability of *at least one* false positive is roughly 34%, not 5%.

2. **Daily peeking over 28 days**: Even with one metric, peeking at a 5% threshold on 28 consecutive days can inflate the false-positive rate to ~72%. Doing this with 8 metrics multiplies the problem further.

The plan claims "5% false-positive rate, which the team has agreed is acceptable," but that rate applies only if you set a single stopping boundary *in advance*, not if you check every morning. This is a classic optional-stopping fallacy.

**What should change:**

- **Use sequential testing** (Wald's SPRT, alpha-spending rules, or mSPRT) instead of fixed p-values with daily peeking, OR
- **Bonferroni correction**: divide the significance threshold by the number of metrics (e.g., 0.05 / 8 ≈ 0.006), or
- **Pre-specify stopping**: decide on a sample size upfront (e.g., 2 weeks), analyze once, and stick to it.

**Secondary gaps:**

- No power analysis; unclear whether 4,000 checkouts/day for 4 weeks is enough to detect a meaningful effect.
- Guardrails use ±2% thresholds without clarifying if that's statistical significance or absolute change; asymmetry with the primary metric's p<0.05.
- "Shipping/payment drop-off" diagnostics may not be comparable post-redesign since those steps are now combined.

The rollback, instrumentation, and assignment strategy are solid.

Read it. The methodology has real problems — the two biggest ones compound each other:

**1. Daily peeking + stop-on-first-significance inflates the false-positive rate far past 5%.** Checking a p-value every morning and stopping the moment it crosses 0.05 is repeated significance testing without any sequential-testing correction (alpha-spending, group-sequential bounds, etc.). Over up to 20 trading days this alone pushes the true false-positive rate well above the stated 5%.

**2. That inflation is compounded by testing all 8 metrics and calling it a win if *any* hits p<0.05.** No multiple-comparisons correction (Bonferroni, FDR) is applied across the 8 metrics. Combined with #1, the actual chance of a false "win" over the four weeks is much higher than the "5%" the doc claims the team signed off on — the doc's headline risk number is wrong.

**3. No minimum sample size or duration floor before a stop is allowed.** The rule lets you ship on day-1 data. That's both a symptom of #1 (smaller samples make premature-stop noise worse) and a separate problem: it doesn't guarantee at least one full week/weekly cycle of data, so day-of-week effects in checkout behavior could masquerade as a treatment effect.

**4. One test type (two-sample z-test) is applied to all 8 metrics, but not all are proportions.** "Completed orders per session," "payment error rate," and drop-off rates are proportions, where a z-test fits. "Revenue per session" and "median checkout duration" are not — a median in particular isn't validly tested with a z-test built for proportions. As written, the dashboard is running the wrong test on at least two metrics.

**5. Guardrails double as win triggers.** The win condition is "any of the eight metrics significant in treatment's favor," and guardrails are among the eight. So a favorable wiggle in, say, payment error rate could ship the redesign even if the actual metric of record (completed orders per session) never moved. Guardrails should only be able to block a ship, not trigger one.

**6. No sample-ratio-mismatch (SRM) check.** Nothing verifies the actual split stays near 50/50. This is the standard tripwire for assignment/bucketing bugs, and its absence means a broken hash or differential bot/exclusion filtering could produce a fake effect that looks like a real one.

**7. The refund-rate guardrail has a built-in blind spot on early stops.** It has a 14-day lag, but the decision rule can trigger a stop on day 1. Orders from the last two weeks of any early stop won't have had time to generate refunds, so the guardrail will read artificially clean right when a fast stop makes it most important.

What's solid: server-side stable-hash assignment (no client flicker), reusing the existing events pipeline instead of adding new instrumentation, the flag-based rollback (tested, no deploy/migration), and scoping out mobile web.

If I were fixing this, the highest-leverage changes are: replace the daily-peek rule with a proper sequential test (or fix the analysis to a single look after a pre-computed sample size), add a Bonferroni/FDR correction across the 8 metrics, split the win condition from the guardrail condition, and add an SRM check.

The plan has a critical timing issue.

The migration drops `full_name` before the rolling deploy completes. During the ~6-minute deploy window, instances running the old release will still be executing `api/signup.py` and `api/profile_update.py` — which write to `full_name`. But that column is already gone. Those instances will throw errors on every signup and profile update.

The fix is to keep `full_name` in the schema during and after the deploy. Two options:

**Option 1** (cleanest): Don't drop `full_name` in this release. In step 1 of the migration, add the new columns and backfill, but leave `full_name` behind. After the deploy completes, all instances are reading/writing the new columns safely. Drop `full_name` in a follow-up release once you're certain rollback isn't needed.

**Option 2** (one-release): Keep `full_name` and do dual writes during deploy. The migration adds the new columns and backfills. The new code writes to both `full_name` and the new columns for a release cycle, ensuring old instances still work if you need to rollback. Drop `full_name` after you've confirmed stability.

Option 1 is simpler and matches the rollout style you already have. You'd just schedule a separate "drop full_name" migration for a later release.

Not sound — there's a real bug in the plan, not just a stylistic concern.

**The core problem: migration and code deploy aren't compatible during the rollout window.**

The migration drops `full_name` *before any new-release instance starts*. But the rolling deploy takes ~6 minutes, during which up to 9 of 12 instances are still running the *old* release — code in `api/serializers.py`, `api/search.py`, `jobs/welcome_email.py`, `reports/weekly_active.py`, `api/signup.py`, and `api/profile_update.py` that all reference `full_name`. That column is gone the moment the migration job finishes, so every one of those old instances will start erroring on the very requests the plan is trying to protect (signup, profile update, profile reads) — for the whole rollout window, not just an edge case.

**This also breaks the rollback plan.** "Roll back to the previous image" assumes the previous image's code is compatible with the current schema. It isn't — `full_name` no longer exists, so a rollback to old code doesn't recover; it just moves the same crash back onto all 12 instances. The "we've practised rollback, six minutes" reassurance doesn't hold here because rollback was never tested against a schema that already dropped the column being read.

**Fix: split into expand/contract across releases**, which is exactly the two-release option the plan considered and rejected:

1. **Release 1** — migration adds `given_name`/`family_name` (nullable) and backfills, but **keeps `full_name`**. No code changes yet, or code changes that read new columns but fall back / dual-write to `full_name`. Old code is unaffected; rollback is safe.
2. **Release 2** — switch the six call sites to `given_name`/`family_name`. `full_name` still exists as a safety net, so both this release and a rollback of it are schema-compatible.
3. **Release 3** (later, once confident) — migration drops `full_name`.

The "doubles the coordination cost" trade-off they cite against two releases is real, but it's not optional here — a single-release expand-and-contract is only safe if old and new code can both run against the *final* schema simultaneously, and that's not true for this change since `full_name` is being removed outright.

Everything else in the plan — timing, backfill-splitting caveat, verification steps — is reasonable and doesn't need changes.

**Critical issue: use NUMERIC/DECIMAL for money, not DOUBLE PRECISION.**

Your ledger sums `DOUBLE PRECISION` amounts to compute balances (line 60). Floating-point accumulation will drift—you'll get 0.01 or 0.99 cent errors that compound and become audit nightmares. Every ledger system that uses float for money regrets it. Switch `amount` in `ledger_entries`, `monthly_price` in `plans`, and `total` in `invoices` to `NUMERIC(19,2)` (or whatever precision your currency needs).

**Secondary: be explicit about foreign key deletes.** If you delete an account, what happens to its subscriptions and ledger entries? Add `ON DELETE CASCADE` or `ON DELETE RESTRICT` to each foreign key so the behavior is clear and documented.

**Tertiary: invoices and ledger_entries aren't linked.** You write an invoice total at close (line 61), but there's no way to audit which ledger entries made up that total. Consider adding a ledger entry ID range, a line-items table, or a checksum so you can reconcile. This matters when disputes come up.

Everything else (status enum, subscription indexes, account/plan structure) looks solid. But fix the DOUBLE PRECISION before you start writing ledger code—changing it later means a migration that touches every financial record.

Short answer: no, fix a few things before building the ledger on this — the money-type choice and the append-only guarantee are the ones that will actually bite.

**Critical**

- `DOUBLE PRECISION` for all monetary columns (`ledger_entries.amount`, `plans.monthly_price`, `invoices.total`). Floats can't represent currency exactly; summing them for a running balance (per the comment at line 60) will drift and eventually produce off-by-a-cent balances that don't reconcile. Use `NUMERIC(12,2)` (or integer minor units, e.g. `BIGINT` cents) instead.
- No sign/amount convention on `ledger_entries.amount`. Nothing says whether a refund is a negative number or a positive one distinguished only by `entry_type` — whoever writes the insert code will guess, and `sum(amount)` silently gives the wrong balance if the convention is inconsistent. Pin it down with a `CHECK` (e.g. charges/adjustments positive, refunds/credits negative, or vice versa) or a generated `signed_amount` column.
- Nothing enforces the ledger being append-only. It's a table like any other — an `UPDATE`/`DELETE` from any code path silently corrupts history. Worth at least revoking `UPDATE`/`DELETE` for the app role, or adding a trigger that rejects them.

**Should fix**

- The balance query in the comment (`SELECT sum(amount) FROM ledger_entries WHERE account_id = $1`) doesn't group by currency, but `currency` is a per-row column with no constraint tying it to a fixed value per account. If an account ever gets entries in two currencies, that query silently sums apples and oranges into a meaningless number.
- No idempotency key on `ledger_entries`. Billing ledgers are normally fed by retriable events (webhook retries, job retries); without a unique external reference, a retry double-writes a charge.
- `occurred_at` is the only timestamp, and it's just "when it happened" — there's no immutable "when it was recorded" column. If `occurred_at` can be backdated (corrections, late-arriving events), you lose the ability to prove insertion order for audit/reconciliation. Consider adding a `created_at` that's never backfilled.
- `invoices` has no link back to the `ledger_entries` it summed (no `invoice_id` on ledger rows, no junction table). Today the only way to know which entries composed an invoice is re-deriving it from `account_id` + date range, which breaks if entries are inserted late or the period logic changes later.

**Minor**

- No unique constraint stopping overlapping `(account_id, period_start, period_end)` invoice periods.
- No `CHECK (amount <> 0)` on ledger entries — zero-amount rows are probably always a bug.
- `ledger_entries.subscription_id` isn't indexed (low priority, only matters if you query by it).

Everything else — FKs, the two status/index choices, `CHAR(2)`/`CHAR(3)` for country/currency — is reasonable and I wouldn't touch it.

Here's the complete flow:

## Normal path (currentToken)
When a request needs a token, it calls `currentToken()`. This checks if the stored access token exists and still has at least 30 seconds left before expiry (the `SKEW_MS` buffer). If it's valid, it returns immediately. If it's missing or expired, it calls `refresh()`.

## Refresh request (refresh)
The refresh starts a POST to `/oauth/token` with the stored refresh token. The critical part is the global `inFlight` variable — if a refresh is already in progress, any other call to `refresh()` returns that same promise rather than starting a new request. This collapses concurrent refresh attempts into a single HTTP call.

## Response handling
- **401 Unauthorized**: The refresh token is invalid or revoked. The code clears the entire store and throws, forcing re-authentication. Any request waiting on this refresh will fail too.
- **Other errors** (4xx/5xx): Throws an error. The request that triggered the refresh will fail, but `inFlight` is cleared so the next request can retry the refresh.
- **Success**: Extracts the new access token and expiry from the response, stores them, and returns the token. If the server sends a new refresh token (rotation), it's updated too.

## Critical timing: the inFlight guard
The key concurrency pattern: imagine two requests come in while the token is expired. Both call `currentToken()`, which calls `refresh()`. The first one starts the fetch and sets `inFlight` to that promise. The second one enters `refresh()`, sees `inFlight` is already set, and immediately returns that same promise. Both requests then await the same network call. When it completes, `.finally()` clears `inFlight` so future refreshes start fresh.

The 30-second skew buffer prevents a race: if the token expires in 5 seconds and two requests come in simultaneously, both would pass the expiry check separately and try to refresh. The skew ensures one sees an almost-expired token and triggers refresh before the other request even gets sent.

Here's the flow in `auth.js`.

**Normal path — `currentToken(store)` (auth.js:6-10)**
1. Reads the cached access token from `store`.
2. If it exists and has more than `SKEW_MS` (30s, line 2) left before `expiresAt`, returns `t.value` directly — no network call.
3. Otherwise (missing, or expiring within 30s) it calls `refresh(store)` and returns whatever that resolves to.

**Refresh — `refresh(store)` (auth.js:12-38)**
4. First checks the module-level `inFlight` variable (line 13). If a refresh is already running, it returns that *same promise* instead of starting a new one — this is the dedup mechanism.
5. If not, it reads the stored refresh token. No refresh token means an immediate throw (`no refresh token; re-auth required`, line 15) — nothing gets assigned to `inFlight` in this case.
6. Otherwise it starts the `fetch('/oauth/token', ...)` POST and immediately assigns the resulting `.then().finally()` chain to `inFlight` (lines 16-37), then returns it.
7. When the response comes back:
   - **Status 401** (line 21): `store.clear()` wipes both the access and refresh tokens, then throws `refresh rejected; re-auth required`.
   - **Other non-ok status** (line 25): throws `refresh failed: <status>`.
   - **OK**: parses the body, writes the new access token with a freshly computed `expiresAt`, and — only if the server sent one (line 31) — rotates the stored refresh token. Resolves with `body.access_token`.
8. Regardless of outcome, `.finally()` (line 34) resets `inFlight = null`, so the *next* call to `refresh()` after this one settles will start a brand-new fetch.

**Two requests refreshing at once**

Because `refresh()` has no `await` before it checks and sets `inFlight`, the whole "check `inFlight`, read the refresh token, fire `fetch`, assign to `inFlight`" sequence runs synchronously in one tick. So if two callers invoke `refresh()` back-to-back (e.g. two `currentToken()` calls in the same microtask), the first call sets `inFlight` before the second call's `if (inFlight)` check runs. Both callers end up awaiting the exact same promise and get the exact same result — one network call serves both. If either caller's `refresh()` invocation happens to land *after* the previous fetch has already settled and cleared `inFlight`, it starts a new fetch instead — that's a real timing edge, not a bug, just worth knowing before you touch the sequencing.

**On a 401 — two different meanings, only one is handled**

- A 401 **from the refresh endpoint itself** (line 21) is fully handled as described above: tokens cleared, error thrown, propagates to every caller waiting on `inFlight`, and the next `refresh()` call fails fast because the refresh token is gone.
- A 401 **from some other API call that used the access token** (e.g. a resource server rejecting it because it was revoked, or a clock-skew edge case) is **not handled anywhere in this file**. There's no wrapper that catches a downstream 401 and forces a refresh — `currentToken()` only checks the locally-cached `expiresAt`. If a caller gets a 401 on an actual API request and just calls `currentToken()` again, it'll hand back the same still-locally-valid token, because nothing here reacts to that failure. If your change involves reacting to 401s from protected requests (not just the refresh call), that path doesn't exist yet and you'd be adding it, not modifying it.

Use a UUID. For sharded systems, UUIDs avoid the coordination overhead of centralized ID generation and distribute naturally across shards without hotspots.

The trade-off: UUIDs are 16 bytes vs 8 for an int64, and slightly slower to index. But on a payments table, the operational simplicity of avoiding cross-shard ID coordination outweighs the storage cost. If you embedded a shard ID in an auto-incrementing integer instead, you'd need that logic at write time and lose the natural ordering an int provides.

UUID (v4 for random distribution, or v7/ULID if you want time-ordering for index locality).

With three regional shards, an auto-incrementing integer needs a central sequence coordinator or per-shard offset ranges — both add coordination overhead or operational fragility. A UUID lets each region generate primary keys independently with no collisions and no cross-region round-trip.

Trade-off: random UUIDs fragment B-tree indexes and hurt insert locality/caching. If that matters, use UUIDv7 or ULID — they're still globally unique and collision-free per-region, but sort roughly by creation time, keeping inserts index-friendly.

- pace error above 15% for two consecutive cycles

That keeps the alert *decision* inside the pure core, so it's covered by the same unit tests and the simulation harness's high-speed replay, and the supervisor's job stays dumb: iterate `result.alerts` and call `alert()`.

**2. Heartbeat missed — can't be built the same way**

This one is structurally different: it's the *absence* of a cycle, so nothing inside a dead or hung loop can raise it. It needs an external watchdog, not more logic inside `govern()` or the supervisor. Standard shape: the supervisor writes a per-tenant "last cycle completed at T" timestamp when it persists state (line 20 already implies this record exists), and a separate process on its own schedule — a small cron/checker, or a dead-man's-switch rule in whatever metrics/alerting system is in place (Prometheus Alertmanager's `absent()`, Datadog monitor, etc.) — pages if that timestamp goes stale beyond some multiple of five minutes, per tenant.

I'd need to know a bit about your setup to give a tailored recommendation, but the main approaches are:

**Application-level logging** (simplest): Intercept every write operation—wrap your ORM/database calls or add middleware—and log `(user_id, operation, resource, timestamp, before/after state)` to an audit table. Works everywhere, but relies on code discipline to avoid gaps.

**Database triggers** (most reliable): Let the database enforce it. On every `INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE`, a trigger writes to an audit log table with the old/new values. Can't be bypassed, but adds database complexity and may hit performance at scale.

**Event sourcing** (most robust): Store every state change as an immutable event. Derive current state by replaying events. Gives you a full history and makes compliance audits trivial, but requires rethinking how you store and query data.

**Change Data Capture** (if using modern databases): Tools like Postgres WAL decoding or database-native CDC stream changes to an audit system. Decouples audit from application code.

The trade-offs: application logging is easiest to add but can have blind spots; triggers are bulletproof but add database load; event sourcing is the "right" architecture but a major refactor; CDC is elegant for distributed systems but requires infrastructure.

The typical approach is a **two-layer cache**: application-level (Redis/Memcached) plus HTTP caching.

**Application layer**: Cache serialized product data with a TTL (e.g., 5–60 minutes). On cache miss, hit the database and store the result. On product update, invalidate that key. Tradeoff: simple to add, but introduces staleness and invalidation complexity.

**HTTP layer**: Set `Cache-Control` headers so browsers and CDNs cache the full response. Use `max-age` for the cache duration and optionally `stale-while-revalidate` to serve stale content while refreshing in the background. Tradeoff: scales to zero database load for repeat visitors, but misses during the TTL after a product update.

**Optional**: Pre-warm the cache on deploys or after product updates, and use a background job to refresh popular items before they expire (prevents thundering herd when a cached item expires).

The choice depends on your product data mutability. If products rarely change and traffic is spread across many product pages, HTTP caching alone may be enough. If updates are frequent or you need freshness within seconds, add Redis with a shorter TTL and smarter invalidation (publish-subscribe on product updates).

Looked at the code — this maps cleanly onto a real fix, not a hypothetical.

**What's actually happening today**

`middleware/security.js` puts `Cache-Control: no-store, no-cache, must-revalidate, private` on *every* response, applied app-wide after the 2024 audit finding on `/account`. The CDN (`CDN.md`) already sits in front of everything and honors origin headers exactly — no path rules, no forced TTLs — which is why its hit rate is 0%: the app is telling it never to cache anything, including `/p/:slug`, which has nothing in common with the page that caused the finding.

`/p/:slug` (`routes/products.js`) reads no session, sets no per-user state, and the comment confirms price/stock/copy are identical for every visitor. Its cost is three sequential DB calls — `productBySlug` (~40ms), `relatedProducts` (~600ms, the four-table join), `stockFor` (~250ms) — matching the ~900ms you're seeing. None of that data is per-user; it only changes when someone edits a product in admin, a few times a day.

**The fix has two layers**

1. **Split the security middleware's policy instead of applying it globally.** `/account` keeps exactly what it has now — `no-store, no-cache, must-revalidate, private` — that finding was real and must stay fixed. `/p` gets its own `Cache-Control: public, max-age=<N>, stale-while-revalidate=<M>`. This alone lets the CDN, which is already correctly positioned, start serving repeat hits with zero app or DB involvement. Given edits happen a few times a day, something like `max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=300` is a reasonable starting point — freshness within a minute, and the SWR window means a cache expiry doesn't force a synchronous slow render, it serves stale and refreshes in the background.

2. **Add an application-level cache (Redis or in-process LRU) in front of `relatedProducts` and `stockFor`, keyed by product id.** The edge cache handles repeat hits per URL, but it doesn't help the first hit, the post-TTL-expiry hit, or a purge — those still go to the app, and `relatedProducts` is the 600ms line item. Caching it by product id (not slug) also dedupes if a product is ever reachable by more than one URL. TTL can mirror or slightly exceed the edge TTL; since edits are infrequent, time-based expiry alone is probably sufficient without wiring up active invalidation.

**Two things worth deciding explicitly rather than defaulting into:**

- *Stock freshness.* If a hot product's cache expires, all concurrent requests for it hitting `stockFor` at once is a stampede risk. `stale-while-revalidate` at the edge plus a single-flight lock at the app-cache layer (only one request repopulates, others get stale or wait) covers this. Separately, if "exact quantity" isn't actually a product requirement and a threshold badge (in stock / low stock / out) is enough, that tolerates a minute of staleness far better than a number does — worth confirming with whoever owns that copy before picking a TTL.
- *Invalidation on publish.* TTL expiry alone means an admin edit takes up to `max-age` to show. If that's not acceptable, the admin tool can call the CDN's purge API and evict the app-cache entry for that product id on save — that's a targeted invalidation, not a new path rule, so it doesn't reopen the "policy lives in two places" objection platform engineering raised last quarter.

Net effect: cold/first-time requests still pay roughly the current ~900ms (minus whatever the app-cache saves), but the overwhelming majority of traffic to a public, rarely-changing page should stop reaching Postgres — or the app — at all.

Rate limiting typically works in layers:

**1. Identification**
Clients are tracked by a key—IP address, API key, user ID, or combination. The key needs to be reliable (e.g., IP works for public endpoints; API key for authenticated clients).

**2. Quota tracking**
A counter tracks how many requests a client has made in a time window. This lives in fast storage (in-memory cache, Redis, or a database with aggressive caching). The counter resets periodically—either sliding window (per-client clock) or fixed window (everyone resets at the same time).

**3. Enforcement**
When a client exceeds their limit, reject the request early with a `429 Too Many Requests` response. This can live at:
- **Reverse proxy/load balancer** (nginx, Cloudflare, AWS API Gateway)—cheapest, stops traffic before it hits your app
- **Application middleware**—gives you control; can rate-limit by fine-grained criteria (per-endpoint, per-user tier)
- **Database layer**—protects your database specifically

**4. Algorithm choice**
- **Token bucket**: Clients get N tokens per window; each request costs 1. Bursty traffic okay, but bounded. Easy to implement.
- **Sliding window**: Strict per-client clock. More accurate but pricier to track.
- **Fixed window**: Simple—reset all clients at T:00, T:01, etc. Risk of "cliff" at boundary where traffic spikes just before reset.

**5. Configuration**
Set limits per tier: free tier (100 req/min), paid (10k req/min), etc. Some systems expose remaining quota in response headers so clients can throttle themselves proactively.

**In practice**: Start at the reverse proxy layer (no app overhead), then add application-level fine-grained limits if you need per-endpoint or per-user-tier control. Redis is standard for the counter store if you have multiple app servers.

**Key: client_id, not IP.** The comment in api.js already flags that clients share NAT'd IPs and one client can call from many addresses — IP-based limiting would both over-block innocent clients on the same IP and under-block the offender if they rotate source addresses. Rate limit on `client_id`, which you already have on every request via the auth lookup.

**Where:** a new middleware in the `/v1` router, right after the auth middleware and before the route handlers — so a throttled request never reaches Postgres (which is already doing an auth-lookup query per request, so it's worth protecting too).

**Algorithm:** since state must be shared across 4 workers × N boxes, it has to live in Redis (already a dependency, so no new infra). A fixed-window counter is cheapest but bursts 2x at window boundaries. Token bucket is smoother and cheap to run in Redis via one Lua script (atomic read-modify-write, avoids races from concurrent workers):

```lua
-- KEYS[1] = "rl:{client_id}", ARGV = {now, rate, burst}
local bucket = redis.call("HMGET", KEYS[1], "tokens", "ts")
local tokens = tonumber(bucket[1]) or tonumber(ARGV[3])
local ts = tonumber(bucket[2]) or tonumber(ARGV[1])
local delta = math.max(0, tonumber(ARGV[1]) - ts) * tonumber(ARGV[2])
tokens = math.min(tonumber(ARGV[3]), tokens + delta)
if tokens < 1 then return 0 end
redis.call("HMSET", KEYS[1], "tokens", tokens - 1, "ts", ARGV[1])
redis.call("EXPIRE", KEYS[1], 60)
return 1
```

**Limits by plan:** `req.client.plan` is already resolved, so the bucket's rate/burst are looked up per plan (a small in-memory or Redis-cached table), giving free-tier clients a tight limit and paid tiers more room, without a schema change.

**Response contract:** on rejection, `429` with a `Retry-After` header (and `X-RateLimit-Limit/Remaining/Reset` on all responses) so well-behaved clients back off instead of retrying immediately and making it worse.

**Failure mode:** decide explicitly whether the limiter fails open or closed if Redis is unreachable. Since Redis already sits on the critical path for sessions, a Redis outage is already a bigger problem — fail open (allow requests, alert) is the safer default so a Redis blip doesn't take down `/v1` entirely.

**For the immediate incident:** find the offending `client_id` from logs/metrics (not IP), and drop in a targeted override — a low temporary bucket limit or an outright block keyed on that client_id — before the general limiter is fully rolled out.

**Optional second layer:** a coarse, unauthenticated-request limiter (per-IP or global) at the load balancer/reverse-proxy level to blunt floods before they even reach a worker — but that's a supplement, not a replacement, for the per-client_id limit, given the shared-NAT issue.

The main options are **polling** (client repeatedly fetches updated data), **Server-Sent Events** (server pushes updates to connected clients), or **WebSockets** (two-way connection for real-time data). Polling is simplest to implement but creates wasted requests; SSE or WebSockets give a real-time feel with the server pushing only when data changes, trading slightly more complexity for better resource efficiency and a snappier dashboard.

For a typical ops dashboard, **SSE is the sweet spot**—the server sends updates when metrics change or on a timer, clients receive them automatically, and you get live-updating without polling overhead or the bidirectional complexity of WebSockets. You'd set up an `/updates` SSE endpoint, have the dashboard open an EventSource connection on load, and re-render whenever new data arrives.

Three ways to do this, in order of effort:

**1. Polling (simplest, often good enough)**
Client re-fetches on an interval (`setInterval` + fetch, or a library like React Query/SWR with `refetchInterval`). No backend changes needed. Fine for data that changes every 30s–few minutes and doesn't need sub-second freshness. Downsides: wasted requests when nothing changed, and updates lag by up to one interval.

**2. Server-Sent Events (SSE)**
Server keeps an open HTTP connection and pushes events when data changes; client uses `EventSource`. One-directional (server to client), which is all a dashboard usually needs. Simpler than WebSockets — plain HTTP, auto-reconnect built into the browser API, works through most proxies/load balancers without special config. Good middle ground.

**3. WebSockets**
Full duplex connection. Worth it if the dashboard also needs to send things back to the server (acknowledging alerts, filtering server-side, etc.) or if you're already running a WebSocket layer elsewhere. Needs a bit more infrastructure: connection management, reconnect/backoff logic, possibly a pub-sub backend (Redis, NATS) to fan out updates if you have multiple server instances.

**How the backend triggers the push (for SSE/WebSockets)**
- If updates come from a database: either poll the DB internally on a short interval and diff, or use DB change streams/triggers (Postgres `LISTEN/NOTIFY`, change-data-capture) to push the moment data changes.
- If updates come from an event stream (Kafka, message queue, metrics pipeline), subscribe the server to that and forward relevant events straight to connected clients.
- For multiple server instances, use a pub-sub layer (Redis pub/sub, NATS) so an update landing on one instance reaches clients connected to another.

**Recommendation**
For an ops dashboard specifically — usually metrics/status changing frequently, one-directional, low-latency but not needing bidirectional interaction — SSE is the sweet spot: much less infra than WebSockets, and far more responsive than polling. Start there unless you already have a WebSocket/pub-sub stack in place, in which case reuse it.

**Client side**, either way: replace whatever fetch-on-mount logic exists with a subscription (`EventSource` or WS `onmessage`) that patches the relevant piece of dashboard state, plus a reconnect/backoff strategy and a fallback poll if the connection drops for too long.

For timeouts on payment charges, you'd typically build retries with:

**Exponential backoff + max attempts**: Start with a short delay (e.g., 1-2 seconds), double it on each retry (2s, 4s, 8s...), and cap at a max delay. After 3-5 attempts, mark it as failed. This avoids hammering a struggling payment processor.

**Async job queue**: Instead of retrying synchronously during the request, write a job (charge attempt) to a queue with a retry policy. The background worker processes it, catches transient errors (timeouts, 5xx), and reschedules itself. Persistent jobs let you retry hours or days later if needed.

**Idempotency keys**: Every charge attempt includes a unique key (often UUID or order ID). The payment processor (Stripe, etc.) uses this to dedupe—if a request succeeds but times out before returning, a retry with the same key won't double-charge.

**Circuit breaker**: If your payment provider has an outage, stop retrying immediately instead of burning through attempts. Once errors stabilize, gradually resume.

**Webhook reconciliation**: Don't trust the retry result alone. After a few hours, query the payment provider's API to confirm the charge actually went through (or failed for a permanent reason). Show the customer the true status, not the timeout message.

**Fallback**: After retries are exhausted, show "payment processing" or "pending" rather than "failed"—keep it queued for manual retry or async completion.

The key insight: **don't retry in the HTTP handler** (the customer won't wait 30 seconds). Move it to async, make it idempotent, and reconcile later.

The core issue: a timeout means you don't actually know whether the charge succeeded on the processor's side, only failed, or is still in flight. Retrying blindly risks double-charging; showing "failed" and giving up risks lying to a customer who was actually charged. The fix has four pieces:

**1. Idempotency keys (the foundation)**
Generate one idempotency key per checkout attempt (not per HTTP call) and send it with every charge request, including retries. Stripe/Adyen/etc. dedupe on this key — if the original request actually went through, a retry with the same key returns the original result instead of creating a second charge. Without this, nothing else below is safe.

**2. Classify the failure before deciding what to do**
- **Definite decline** (insufficient funds, card declined) → don't retry, show the real reason.
- **Definite processor error** (5xx, rate limited) → safe to retry.
- **Timeout / network error** → outcome unknown. This is the case you're describing, and it needs different handling than "failed."

**3. A state machine, not a boolean**
Track each charge attempt in your own DB as `pending` / `succeeded` / `failed` / `unknown`, not just success/fail. On timeout, set it to `pending` (or `unknown`), not `failed`. Then:
- Retry synchronously a couple of times with the same idempotency key, exponential backoff + jitter, inside a small time budget (e.g. under 10s total) so you're not blocking the request indefinitely.
- If still unresolved, don't fail the checkout — hand off to async reconciliation: a background job that calls the processor's lookup/status endpoint for that idempotency key, and a webhook listener (`charge.succeeded`/`charge.failed`) as the source of truth, since the webhook will arrive even though your synchronous call timed out.

**4. Customer-facing behavior**
Only show "payment failed" for genuine declines. For a timeout, show something honest like "confirming your payment" and resolve it via polling or a follow-up notification once the async reconciliation lands — never re-prompt the customer to re-enter their card while a charge might still be in flight, that's how double charges happen.

Separately: alert on timeout rate distinct from decline rate — a timeout spike is a processor/network problem, not a customer payment problem, and gets buried if it's lumped into a generic "payment failed" metric.

I'd recommend starting with a backend search API endpoint that queries your product table with a `WHERE name LIKE %query% OR description LIKE %query%` filter, paired with a debounced input on the frontend. This is simple to ship and works fine for moderate catalogs. The tradeoff: it doesn't scale well past a few thousand products and can't rank by relevance — if you anticipate thousands of SKUs or need fuzzy matching (typo tolerance), you'd want a full-text search engine like Meilisearch or Postgres's native full-text search, which adds setup overhead but gives you relevance tuning and performance.

**Key pieces:** debounced search input → API call to `/products/search?q=...` → backend filters and returns paginated results → render results with highlighting. For polish, add loading states, empty results messaging, and maybe category/filter chips depending on your data structure.

Given the scale here (schema.sql says ~38k products, growing by a few hundred/month, on Postgres 16), Postgres's built-in full-text search is the right tool — no need for Elasticsearch/Meilisearch/Algolia as a separate service to run and keep in sync.

**1. Schema change** — add a generated `tsvector` column weighting name above description, plus a GIN index:

```sql
ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN search_vector tsvector
    GENERATED ALWAYS AS (
        setweight(to_tsvector('english', name), 'A') ||
        setweight(to_tsvector('english', description), 'B')
    ) STORED;

CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY products_search_idx ON products USING GIN (search_vector);
```

Being a generated column, it stays in sync automatically on insert/update — no trigger or app-side maintenance. `CONCURRENTLY` avoids locking `products` during index build (not strictly needed at 38k rows, but cheap insurance on a live table).

**2. Query** — `websearch_to_tsquery` parses free-text input the way users actually type ("wireless mouse", quoted phrases, `-excluded`), so the "few words" from the user go straight in without you writing a parser:

```sql
SELECT id, sku, name, price_cents,
       ts_rank(search_vector, query) AS rank
FROM products, websearch_to_tsquery('english', $1) query
WHERE active AND search_vector @@ query
ORDER BY rank DESC, name
LIMIT 50 OFFSET $2;
```

**3. Route** — new `GET /products/search?q=...&page=...` in `routes/products.js`, mirroring the existing paging pattern.

**Tradeoff worth flagging:** `to_tsvector` stems words (run/running/runs match) but won't catch typos or partial prefixes ("wireles" won't match "wireless"). If that matters for this catalog, pair it with `pg_trgm` (`CREATE EXTENSION pg_trgm` + a GIN trigram index on `name`) and blend trigram similarity into the ranking or use it as a fallback when the tsquery returns nothing. I'd ship without it first and add it only if search-quality feedback calls for it — it's extra index weight and query complexity for a catalog this size.

This scales comfortably past 38k rows into the low millions before you'd need to reach for a dedicated search engine.

A marketplace photo upload system typically combines these pieces:

**Client side:** Capture from camera or gallery, compress on-device (resize to ~1-2MB), show preview while uploading.

**Upload mechanism:** The main choice is presigned URLs (client uploads directly to S3 with a temporary signed URL from your server) vs. server-mediated (client posts to your backend, which handles storage). Presigned URLs save server bandwidth and are standard for user-generated content; server-mediated gives you more control for validation and abuse prevention.

**Processing pipeline:** After upload, generate thumbnails and resized variants (listing grid view, detail view, etc.) using a queue job (Redis + worker or pub/sub). Store the original and variants in a CDN-backed bucket (S3 + CloudFront or equivalent).

**Data model:** Store photo metadata (order, listing ID, upload timestamp) in your database with references to the S3 keys; clients load the CDN URLs.

**Key tradeoffs:** Presigned uploads are simpler but require browser-native S3 integration; server-mediated is easier to audit but costs more bandwidth. Processing variants is slower but essential for performance on mobile networks viewing the listing.

Here's a practical architecture for phone-camera-size photo uploads on a listing:

**1. Client-side capture & pre-processing**
- Accept via `<input type="file" accept="image/*" capture="environment">` on mobile web, or native camera/picker in an app.
- Phone photos run 3–12MB at 3000–4500px on the long edge, and iPhones default to HEIC. Before upload, downscale in-browser/in-app (canvas or a library like `browser-image-compression`) to something like 2000px max edge / ~80% JPEG quality — cuts upload size 5–10x with no visible quality loss for listing photos, and sidesteps HEIC decode issues in downstream image libraries by re-encoding to JPEG/WebP client-side.
- Read EXIF orientation and bake it into the pixels (or strip it) before upload — phone photos routinely display sideways if you don't handle this.

**2. Transport**
- Don't proxy raw bytes through your app server. Have the server issue a short-lived presigned URL (S3/GCS/R2), and have the client PUT directly to object storage. Keeps your app server free of multi-MB request bodies and scales trivially.
- Flow: client requests upload URL for `listingId` → server checks auth (seller owns listing) and returns a presigned PUT URL + a final object key → client uploads → client notifies server "upload complete" with the key → server records it.

**3. Server-side processing**
- On the "upload complete" callback (or via an S3 event trigger), kick a background job that:
  - Validates it's actually an image and within size/dimension limits (defend against a malicious client bypassing your pre-resize).
  - Strips EXIF GPS/metadata (privacy — sellers' phone GPS location shouldn't leak) unless you intentionally want geotagging.
  - Generates a small set of derivatives: thumbnail (~200px), listing-card (~600px), full-view (~1600px), stored as WebP/JPEG.
  - Writes rows to a `listing_photos` table: `id, listing_id, storage_key, width, height, sort_order, status, created_at`.
- Do this async so the upload UI doesn't block on processing; show the photo immediately from a client-side blob preview, then swap to the CDN URL once processing finishes.

**4. Data model & ordering**
- `listing_photos` linked to `listings` by foreign key, with `sort_order` for drag-to-reorder and a `is_cover` flag or just "position 0 = cover."
- Enforce limits server-side: max photo count per listing, max file size, allowed MIME types — never trust client-side checks alone.

**5. Delivery**
- Serve derivatives through a CDN in front of the object storage bucket, not direct bucket URLs.

**6. UX details worth planning for**
- Multi-select/multi-capture with per-photo progress bars and retry-on-failure (mobile networks drop mid-upload often).
- Allow reordering and deleting before/after publish.
- Show a client-side preview instantly (from the local file) while the real upload/processing happens in the background, so the seller isn't staring at spinners.

The bug is in how the middleware handles Redis failures. When `redis.incr(key)` fails (line 12 in limiter.js), it returns `null` instead of throwing (redis-client.js, line 22). 

Then on line 17 of limiter.js:
```javascript
if (count > MAX_REQUESTS) {
```

When `count` is `null`, the comparison `null > 100` evaluates to `false`, so the rate limit check passes silently. Every request gets through if Redis is unavailable or erroring.

The middleware fails open instead of failing closed. A Redis outage, timeout, or any error disables rate limiting entirely—all 12,000 requests likely came while Redis was down or flaky. You need to either reject requests when Redis fails (fail closed) or at minimum track the error separately from the null return so the limiter can distinguish between "limit not exceeded" and "couldn't check the limit."

redis-client.js swallows every Redis error and returns `null` instead of throwing (its explicit design goal — "a Redis blip must never turn into a 500"). limiter.js never accounts for that: `redis.incr(key)` can resolve to `null`, and `null > MAX_REQUESTS` is `false` in JavaScript, so `count > 100` fails open and `next()` runs unblocked.

So any Redis hiccup — a timeout (only 200ms `connectTimeout`), a dropped connection, `maxRetriesPerRequest: 1` exhausted — makes every request during that blip bypass the limit entirely, with no logging in limiter.js itself to show it happened (only `redis.error`/`metrics.increment` on the client side). A client hammering the endpoint during sustained Redis instability, or one that triggers enough load to cause Redis latency/timeouts itself, could ride `null` responses straight through to 12,000 requests with zero 429s.

`git restore --staged` unstages files—it removes them from the staging area (index) while keeping the changes in your working directory. It's the opposite of `git add`.

For example:
- `git add file.txt` stages the file
- `git restore --staged file.txt` unstages it (but the file's changes remain on disk)

This is the modern alternative to `git reset HEAD file.txt`.

`git restore --staged <file>` unstages the file — it removes it from the index (undoes `git add`) but leaves your working directory changes untouched. It's the modern equivalent of `git reset HEAD <file>`.

Keep both keys active during a transition period. Here's the pattern:

**Dual-key verification:** Store both the old and new signing keys, and accept JWTs signed by either during a grace period (typically the lifetime of your longest-lived tokens, often 7–30 days). Start signing *new* tokens immediately with the new key. After the grace period, stop accepting the old key.

The implementation:
- Add the new key alongside the old one in your signing key store
- Update your JWT verification to check against both keys
- Start issuing new tokens with the new key
- After the grace period, remove the old key from verification

**Trade-off:** Tokens don't expire early (no logout), but you carry both keys in production for a while. The window is bounded by your token lifetime, so it's not indefinite—just long enough for all old tokens to naturally expire.

**Variations if you want tighter control:**
- **Force refresh on next use:** Still sign with the new key immediately, but when a client presents an old-key token, accept it once and return a new token signed with the new key.
- **Staged key replacement:** If you control all clients, push clients to refresh their tokens before you rotate, minimizing the dual-key window.

The dual-key approach is simplest and most robust for web applications where you can't coordinate exact client behavior.

The standard approach is a **dual-key overlap window** using the `kid` (Key ID) header, so old tokens keep verifying while new tokens get signed with the new key.

**Steps:**

1. **Add a `kid` to every token you sign.** If you're not already doing this, add it now — it's what makes rotation possible later.
2. **Generate the new key but don't cut over signing yet.** Add it to your verification key set (JWKS if asymmetric, or a keyed secret store if HMAC) alongside the old key, tagged with its own `kid`.
3. **Update your verifier to look up the key by `kid`** instead of assuming a single static key. It should accept tokens signed by either the old or new key during the overlap period.
4. **Switch signing to the new key.** New tokens now carry the new `kid`; existing unexpired tokens still carry the old one and still verify.
5. **Keep the old key in the verification set until every token signed with it has expired** — i.e., for at least your longest token TTL (access token TTL, or refresh token TTL if you validate those the same way). No active session gets rejected because the old key is still honored until it's provably unused.
6. **Remove the old key** from the verification set once that window has passed.

**Practical notes:**
- If you use asymmetric signing (RS256/ES256), publish both keys on your JWKS endpoint during the overlap and make sure clients/services cache with a reasonable TTL (not indefinitely) so they pick up the new key in time.
- If you use HMAC (HS256), there's no public JWKS, so this means your own services need a `kid` → secret lookup instead of one hardcoded secret.
- Automate this as a pipeline (add key → wait TTL → cut over signing → wait TTL → remove old key) rather than doing it by hand, so rotation stays routine instead of an incident.
- If refresh tokens are long-lived (days/weeks), that's your binding constraint on the overlap window, not the access token TTL.
